headline: Seven bullets at Fort Hood. He doubts the livestream.
summary: Alonzo Lunsford was shot seven times at Fort Hood in 2009. He told the BBC the firing squad fits Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 soldiers there, and he plans to be in the room on December 3. The livestream Hegseth promised is another matter: "not something you should view for entertainment purposes." Legal experts say it may never happen.

cover_question.q: Why do they want people to watch?

cover_answer: Hegseth says so people see the consequences.
table_question: Does a punishment count less if nobody sees it?

5-7.script: A soldier killed 13 people at an Army base in Texas in 2009, long before you were born. A court said he must die for it, and that happens in December. The Army wants it on a screen, like a TV that can stay off, and one of the men he shot says no. Nobody has to watch, we won't, and the grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: Shielded. If it reaches them: before you were born, and a screen that stays off.
5-7.why_long: Shielded: a six-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script gives no method and no picture, only a date far off and a screen that stays off. The man who was shot and still says no is the anchor: a grown-up on the child's side. Expect "will you watch?" No.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: In 2009 Army Major Nidal Hasan shot 13 soldiers dead at Fort Hood, Texas. A court sentenced him to death, Trump signed off, and the firing squad is set for December 3. Hegseth added a camera. Alonzo Lunsford, shot seven times, wants the call to stand and says the crowd should not get the replay.
8-12.why: The chain of rules, then the step nobody required: the camera.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out whether adults apply rules consistently, so the script hands them the chain: a conviction, the president's signature, a date. The camera is the step nobody required, and the referee's replay is the mechanism they know. Lunsford draws the line at the crowd. Expect "would you watch?" No, and say why.

13-17.script: Who gets a say in a punishment: the state, or the people it hurt? Alonzo Lunsford, shot seven times at Fort Hood, will be in the room on December 3 and says the public should not be. Second: Senator Tillis, a Republican, says public executions are what dictators do.
13-17.why: One survivor, two true things. Then a Republican senator's no.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: a man shot seven times wants the sentence carried out, and that same man says the public should not watch. The script gives Hegseth's reason in his words and Tillis's objection in his, so the argument is between adults who agree on the sentence. Expect "would you watch?" Answer first.

5-7.a: No. That screen stays off in our house. One of the men he shot says kids shouldn't see it.

8-12.q: Why do they want people to watch?
8-12.a: Hegseth says so people see there are consequences. Lunsford says it isn't entertainment.
Maybe. Legal experts told the BBC it could be challenged in court.

13-17.q: Should the public get to watch?
13-17.a: Hegseth: to show consequences. Lunsford: families yes, public no.

13-17.q: Has he forgiven the man who shot him?
13-17.a: Yes. "I cannot heal if I don't forgive him," he said.
